svg.title: Three keys for BGP as PE-CE: as-override, allowas-in and site of origin, and when each applies
svg.desc: Three columns, each named for the symptom it solves. Column one, as-override: the customer edge rejects a route because it sees its own AS number in the AS path; the provider edge rewrites the AS path before advertising so the loop check passes, at the cost of losing that loop evidence. Column two, allowas-in: the customer edge is allowed to accept its own AS number up to a configured count, which keeps the path intact and moves the decision to the customer side. Column three, site of origin: a dual-homed site would learn its own prefix back through the provider; the community marks the origin site so the re-injection is dropped. A bottom band states the selection rule: use as-override only when the provider controls both ends, allowas-in when the customer does, and always pair either with site of origin at sites that have a backdoor.
svg.text: Three keys, three different symptoms — applying the wrong one hides a loop instead of stopping it
All three exist because a customer's AS number must survive a provider it does not control
KEY 1
as-override
Symptom: the CE rejects a route it should
accept, because its own AS is in the path.
The PE rewrites the AS path before sending,
replacing the customer's AS with its own.
Cost: the loop evidence is erased. A real
loop will no longer be detected here.
Configured on the PE, applies to all sites
behind that PE.
KEY 2
allowas-in
Symptom: the same rejection, but the fix is
allowed on the customer side instead.
The CE accepts its own AS up to N times, so
the path is preserved and the decision is local.
Cost: the customer must configure it, and the
count must be justified, not guessed.
Configured on the CE. Better when the two
sides belong to different organisations.
KEY 3
site of origin
Symptom: a dual-homed site learns its own
prefix back through the provider.
The community marks where the route started,
so the site drops what it just sent.
Cost: one more attribute to plan per site, and
a duplicate value silently breaks reachability.
Required whenever a backdoor exists — with
or without the other two keys.
The rule of thumb
Provider controls both ends of the session → as-override is simpler. Customer owns the CE → allowas-in moves the change to the party that owns it.
Either way, add site of origin at any site with a second path, or the loop returns through the backdoor instead of the provider.
The failure this prevents: a dual-homed site's backdoor link carries its own prefix back into the VPN. The two copies compete, EIGRP metrics climb,
and traffic ping-pongs between the provider and the backdoor. Every few minutes the path changes, latency doubles, and the graph shows nothing
wrong because no interface ever went down. This is what as-override and allowas-in alone cannot fix, and what site of origin exists for.
Sequence for a new dual-homed site: SoO first, then the AS path tool. Never the other way round.
